content: Cod liver oil is extracted from the livers of codfish and is commonly used as a nutritional supplement. Historically, it was frequently administered to children. It is one of the richest sources of omega-3 fatty acids and provides significant amounts of vitamins A and D. Cod liver oil is often consumed to alleviate joint pain and stiffness associated with arthritis. Additionally, clinical studies have demonstrated its beneficial effects on cardiovascular, skeletal, and neurological health, as well as its ability to improve the condition of skin, hair, and nails. However, some rheumatologists attribute these benefits to a placebo effect and question the validity of the supporting studies. The flavor and aroma of cod liver oil vary depending on its quality, ranging from a mild sardine-like taste to a strong, unpleasant odor reminiscent of rotten fish and rancid oil. High-quality cod liver oil is described as a pale-yellow, thin, oily liquid with a slightly fishy but not rancid odor and a bland, slightly fishy taste. To improve its palatability, it is now often flavored with citrus or mint essences. Cod liver oil is produced by steaming cod livers and then pressing or decanting them to extract the oil. In contrast, fish oils are derived from the cooked whole-body tissues of fatty fish during the production of fish meal. While cod liver oil and fish oil share similarities, their compositions differ. Fish oil contains significantly lower levels of vitamins A and D compared to cod liver oil. This difference can pose a challenge, as achieving therapeutic levels of EPA and DHA from cod liver oil may require exceeding the recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for vitamins A and D. Since these vitamins are fat-soluble, excessive intake can accumulate in the body and become toxic. The body naturally synthesizes vitamin D when exposed to sunlight. To avoid vitamin D overdose while benefiting from both oils, it is recommended to take cod liver oil during late fall and winter and switch to fish oil during spring and summer. The optimal dosage and timing depend on seasonal sun exposure and natural vitamin D production. To ensure proper vitamin D levels and avoid deficiencies or overdosing, regular testing is advised. However, many experts believe the RDA for vitamin D is underestimated, and a significant portion of adults fail to meet it. Pregnant women who consume cod liver oil have been shown to have infants with a reduced risk of developing juvenile type 1 diabetes. This protective effect is specific to cod liver oil and is not observed in mothers taking multivitamin supplements. Additionally, nursing mothers who take cod liver oil improve the fatty acid profile of their breast milk, promoting optimal brain development in their infants. It also increases vitamin A levels in breast milk, which helps prevent infections. However, cod liver oil does not enhance the vitamin D content of breast milk. Pregnant women should exercise caution and avoid excessive consumption, as research from Iceland indicates that high intake of cod liver oil is associated with a nearly fivefold increased risk of gestational hypertension. In Newfoundland, cod liver oil was historically used as the liquid base for traditional red ochre paint, which was commonly applied to outbuildings and work structures associated with the cod fishery. Caution is advised when consuming cod liver oil and other fish-based supplements, as they may contain elevated levels of toxins such as mercury and polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), which are increasingly found in fish. Some supplement manufacturers regularly test cod liver oil for purity, while others do not.
